title: Assembly in Arduino C++: integration and performance

questions.prompt: Can 8051 assembly instructions be used in an Arduino Uno sketch?
options: No; the Uno R3 commonly uses an AVR CPU with a different instruction set.
Yes; every Arduino uses an 8051 CPU.
Yes, if the instruction is inside setup().
Only when loop() is empty.
questions.answer: No; the Uno R3 commonly uses an AVR CPU with a different instruction set.
questions.explanation: Assembly must match the board's processor architecture and toolchain.

questions.prompt: In the AVR-GCC example, what does the `+r` constraint mean?
options: The operand is read and written in a general-purpose register.
The operand is a compile-time immediate constant only.
The operand is stored in flash and cannot change.
The assembly may use any undeclared register.
questions.answer: The operand is read and written in a general-purpose register.
questions.explanation: The plus modifier marks a read-write output operand and r requests a register.

questions.prompt: Does `asm volatile` make surrounding C++ variables volatile or an operation atomic?
options: No; it asks GCC to retain the assembly statement, but those are separate properties.
Yes, both automatically.
It makes all interrupts safe.
It disables every compiler optimization.
questions.answer: No; it asks GCC to retain the assembly statement, but those are separate properties.
questions.explanation: Inline-assembly volatility does not declare C++ volatile objects, atomicity, or a full memory barrier.

questions.prompt: Which claim about assembly speed is correct?
options: There is no general guarantee; optimized C++ may compile to the same or better instructions.
Assembly is always faster than C++.
C++ is always faster than assembly.
Source-code line count determines execution time.
questions.answer: There is no general guarantee; optimized C++ may compile to the same or better instructions.
questions.explanation: Compare generated machine code and measure equivalent, observable work on the target.

questions.prompt: What is needed for a meaningful C++ versus assembly benchmark?
options: Same target, compiler and flags, inspect disassembly, prevent dead-code removal, and use suitable repeated timing.
Compare two unrelated boards once with a stopwatch.
Measure only source-code length.
Remove all observable outputs so the compiler can optimize freely.
questions.answer: Same target, compiler and flags, inspect disassembly, prevent dead-code removal, and use suitable repeated timing.
questions.explanation: A controlled comparison must measure equivalent work and account for optimization and measurement overhead.
